propositions.text: The October 25, 2023 second review refusal failed to account for her financial situation
propositions.quote: She seeks judicial review of the October 25, 2023, second review refusal, which she says failed to account for her financial situation.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring has not persuaded me that CRA acted unreasonably in refusing relief from penalties and interest
propositions.quote: she has not persuaded me that the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) acted unreasonably in refusing to grant her relief from the penalties and interest she owes.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring may have a good case for a payment plan reflecting her current circumstances
propositions.quote: while Ms. Sherring may have a good case for entering into a payment plan that reflects her current circumstances

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says second review refusal failed to consider her finances; court finds CRA was not unreasonable; notes she may have a good payment plan case.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring is 71, English instructor in Saskatchewan, filed 2011-2016 returns late, CRA issued assessments with penalties and interest in 2018
propositions.quote: Ms. Sherring is a 71-year-old English language instructor living in Saskatchewan. She did not file her 2011 – 2016 personal tax returns on time, and as a result, the CRA issued notices of tax assessment in 2018 that included arears interest and filing penalties for those years.

propositions.text: She filed 2013-2016 returns later, CRA amended assessments but penalties and interest remained
propositions.quote: Although she subsequently filed tax returns for the 2013-2016 tax years, which resulted in the CRA issuing amended notices of assessment, the penalties and arears interest amounts remained unchanged.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Ms. Sherring's age, occupation, late filing of 2011-2016 returns, and CRA assessments with penalties and interest.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring filed 2017 and 2019 returns late; CRA issued assessments with penalties and interest
propositions.quote: Ms. Sherring again filed her tax returns late for the 2017 and 2019 tax years. The CRA again issued notices of assessment that included arrears interest and late filing penalties.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Ms. Sherring filed 2017 and 2019 returns late and received assessments with penalties and interest.

propositions.text: In April 2022, Ms. Sherring requested relief from penalties and interest for 2006-2021 tax years under Income Tax Act s 220(3.1)
propositions.quote: In April 2022, Ms. Sherring requested relief from penalties and interest owing in respect of the 2006 through 2021 tax years. The request was made pursuant to subsection 220(3.1) of the Income Tax Act, RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp) which grants the Minister discretionary authority to provide relief from tax penalties and interest.

propositions.text: She based her request on financial hardship, medical problems and COVID-19
propositions.quote: Ms. Sherring based her request on what she said were her financial hardship, medical problems and COVID-19.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Ms. Sherring requested relief under Income Tax Act citing financial hardship, medical issues, and COVID-19.

propositions.text: CRA could only consider relief for penalties and interest accrued in 10 years before request, excluding 2006-2010
propositions.quote: The decision maker noted that the CRA could only consider relief of penalties and interest accrued in the 10 years before the request was made (thus excluding tax years 2006-2010)

propositions.text: No penalties or interest related to 2007-2009 tax years
propositions.quote: and observed that there were no penalties or interest related to the 2007-2009 tax years.

propositions.text: For 2011-2021, Ms. Sherring was not prevented from meeting filing and remitting obligations; relief not warranted
propositions.quote: As for the 2011-2021 tax years, the CRA found that Ms. Sherring had not been prevented from meeting her filing and remitting obligations and relief was therefore not warranted.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found relief limited to last 10 years, no penalties 2007-2009, and no prevention from filing 2011-2021, so relief denied.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring requested second review citing financial hardship, illness, emotional and mental distress, supported by letter and medical documentation of 2019 leg fracture
propositions.quote: Ms. Sherring requested a second review of her request for relief from interest and penalties related to the 2011-2021 tax years. She based her request on her financial hardship, illness and emotional and mental distress, and she supported it with a letter, written representations and medical documentation regarding a leg fracture that occurred in 2019.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant requested second review citing financial hardship, illness, distress, supported by letter and medical proof of 2019 leg fracture.

propositions.text: Second review decision-maker refused relief again
propositions.quote: The CRA decision maker who conducted the second review again refused Ms. Sherring’s tax relief request.

propositions.text: Decision-maker noted no doctor consultation for mental health, so no documentation to support claim
propositions.quote: The decision maker observed that by Ms. Sherring’s own admission she had not spoken with a doctor about her mental health issues and therefore had no documentation to support her claim.

propositions.text: Leg fracture occurred June 1, 2019, healed by October 2, 2019, no bearing on ability to comply for prior eight years
propositions.quote: The decision maker further noted that according to the evidence Ms. Sherring’s leg fracture occurred on June 1, 2019, and was healed by October 2, 2019. The decision maker found that the 2019 leg injury had no bearing on Ms. Sherring’s ability to comply with her tax obligations for the eight preceding tax years.

paragraphs.summary: Second review decision-maker refused relief, noting no mental health documentation and leg fracture healed quickly, no impact on prior compliance.

propositions.text: Financial hardship means prolonged inability to provide necessities and extraordinary circumstance preventing timely filing or payment
propositions.quote: As for Ms. Sherring’s assertion of financial difficulties, the decision maker explained that in the relief context, financial hardship involves a “prolonged inability to provide necessities,” and requires an “extraordinary circumstance” preventing a taxpayer from filing and/or paying taxes on time.

propositions.text: Evidence showed Ms. Sherring funded renovations, sold a house, paid off credit, bought a car, contributed over $70,000 to RRSPs 2019-2022
propositions.quote: The evidence before the CRA showed that Ms. Sherring had funded renovations for two houses, sold a house, paid off a line of credit, bought a car, and contributed over $70,000 to her Registered Retirement Savings Plan accounts between 2019-2022.

propositions.text: Decision-maker found Ms. Sherring was not experiencing financial hardship and was not prevented from meeting filing obligations by circumstances beyond her control
propositions.quote: Based on this evidence, the decision maker found that Ms. Sherring was not experiencing financial hardship and was not prevented from meeting her filing obligations due to circumstances beyond her own control.

paragraphs.summary: Decision-maker explained financial hardship test, found evidence showed no hardship, and Ms. Sherring was not prevented from filing by extraordinary circumstances.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring alleges CRA misunderstood her financial circumstances and failed to consider age, physical limitation, and employment ability
propositions.quote: She alleges that the CRA misunderstood her financial circumstances and failed to consider her age, physical limitation and ability to continue employment.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant alleges CRA misunderstood her finances and failed to consider age, physical limits, and employment ability.

propositions.text: Standard of review is reasonableness; decision must be justified, intelligible, transparent, and reflect evidence (Vavilov)
propositions.quote: The standard of review applicable to the CRA second reviewer’s decision is reasonableness. A reasonable decision is one that is “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker” (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 85 [Vavilov]). To be reasonable, an administrative decision must be justified, intelligible and transparent (Vavilov at para 99). It must reflect the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Court states standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov, requiring justification, intelligibility, transparency, and evidence reflection.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring spoke at length about obstacles including financial, physical, emotional challenges
propositions.quote: During the hearing of this judicial review, Ms. Sherring spoke at length about the obstacles she has faced over the years, including financial, physical, and emotional challenges.

propositions.text: Court's role is to review CRA decision based on record; cannot interfere unless decision unreasonable or procedurally unfair
propositions.quote: my role as a reviewing judge is to examine the decision of the CRA in light of the record that was before it. Unless the decision is unreasonable based on that record, or was reached in a procedurally unfair way, I cannot interfere with it, even if I might have weighed the evidence differently.

propositions.text: Court sympathizes with Ms. Sherring but must apply standard of review
propositions.quote: I sympathize with Ms. Sherring. However, as I explained during the hearing, my role as a reviewing judge is to examine the decision of the CRA in light of the record that was before it.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Ms. Sherring's challenges but explains its role is to review CRA decision for reasonableness and fairness only.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring has not shown CRA second review decision was unreasonable
propositions.quote: Ms. Sherring has not persuaded me that the CRA second review decision was unreasonable.

propositions.text: Decision-maker engaged with submissions, reviewed evidence, and made rational, clearly articulated conclusion within discretion
propositions.quote: The decision maker engaged with the submissions, reviewed the evidence, and came to a clearly articulated, rational conclusion that reflected the scope of discretion available under the law.

propositions.text: No valid basis to disturb CRA decision
propositions.quote: There is no valid basis upon which to disturb the CRA’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds CRA decision reasonable, engaged evidence, rational, and no basis to disturb it.

propositions.text: Application dismissed
propositions.quote: While I must therefore dismiss this application,

propositions.text: Respondent's counsel acknowledged Ms. Sherring may negotiate a payment plan with CRA reflecting her current financial situation
propositions.quote: as acknowledged by counsel for the Respondent, it remains open to Ms. Sherring to put her full circumstances, properly supported by evidence, before the CRA in support of a request to negotiate a workable payment plan that reflects her present financial situation.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses application but notes Ms. Sherring may negotiate a payment plan with CRA supported by evidence.

propositions.text: Respondent's request for costs dismissed due to Ms. Sherring's circumstances
propositions.quote: The Respondent’s request for costs is dismissed in light of Ms. Sherring’s circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses Respondent's costs request due to Ms. Sherring's circumstances.

propositions.text: Ms. Sherring named incorrect party as Respondent; Attorney General of Canada should be named
propositions.quote: Finally, the Respondent notes that Ms. Sherring, who is not represented by counsel, has named the incorrect party as the Respondent in this matter. I agree. Pursuant to Rule 303 of the Federal Courts Rules, SOR/98-106, the Attorney General of Canada should be named as the Respondent.

propositions.text: Style of cause amended to name Attorney General of Canada as Respondent; application dismissed; parties bear own costs
propositions.quote: The style of cause shall be amended accordingly. JUDGMENT in T-2564-23 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The style of cause is amended to identify the Attorney General of Canada as the Respondent. The application is dismissed. The parties are responsible for their own costs.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues and court agrees Ms. Sherring named wrong Respondent; style amended; application dismissed; parties bear own costs.
